title: Winter outcrop loss predicted interior AOU gain only in the North Pacific; in four other subtropical gyres no ventilated class lost much outcrop and AOU did not follow (WOA23, GLODAP, 1985-2021)
abstract: Question: is the North Pacific (NP) finding that a density class which loses winter outcrop area gains AOU in the interior a general law of thermocline ventilation? Approach: a pre-specified out-of-sample test in the North Atlantic, South Pacific, South Atlantic and South Indian gyres for sigma0 classes 25.6-27.2. Outcrop areas came from World Ocean Atlas 2023 decadal late-winter surface T and S (change R, 1975-1994 to 1995-2014). Interior AOU changes (2005-2021 minus 1985-1999) came from 115,317 GLODAPv2.2023 bottle samples (512 cruises), matched in 5 x 10 degree cells, with cruise bootstrap. Results: outside the NP, R did not predict AOU change (Spearman rho -0.11, n = 59 units, one-sided p = 0.55 under a circular-shift null). The NP slope gave an out-of-sample R^2 of -0.17. The null held for two other timings and for thermal-only outcrops from WOA23, HadISST1 and COBE-SST2 (rho -0.14 to +0.19). In the NP the control held (rho -0.84; AOU +7.7 and +8.2 umol/kg on 26.5 and 26.6, which lost most outcrop). Surface water with sigma0 >= 26.5 lost 75% of its area in the NP but only 2-10% elsewhere, and only 2 of 59 out-of-sample units had |R| >= 0.2. The late-winter surface became 0.04-0.10 kg/m3 lighter in all gyres, but gyre-mean AOU changes were +3.8 (NP), +8.1 (NA), +0.5 (SP), -3.0 (SA) and +1.8 (SI) umol/kg. A lightening-based shift law predicted gains in all gyres and failed in the SA and SP (exploratory). Conclusion: the outcrop mechanism is a North Pacific threshold effect: a low surface-density ceiling near 26.6 let lightening remove whole classes. It is not a global law. Limitations: sparse pre-2005 Southern Hemisphere surface data (7-25% of cells), decadal resolution, few SH cruises, box domains.

Text: rho of outcrop change R with AOU change, and the lightening.

Outcrop change R against interior AOU change for each gyre-class unit (error bars: bootstrap SE). Dashed: the North Pacific slope through the origin. Labels: classes with |R| >= 0.2. Only the North Pacific shows the predicted negative relation.
Gyre-mean late-winter surface lightening of the outcrop area against the mean AOU change over classes 25.6-27.2: observed (orange circles) and shift-law prediction (open squares).

citations.reason: We test out of sample, in four other gyres, its finding that O2 on sigma0 26.5 follows the winter outcrop area; the relation holds only in the North Pacific.
We use its WOA23 decadal late-winter outcrop method and extend it to five gyres and all classes 25.6-27.2; we confirm the North Pacific 26.5 outcrop loss.
Our GLODAP control confirms the largest North Pacific AOU gain on the classes that stopped outcropping (26.5-26.6).
Its outcrop-scaled renewal is a North Pacific result; we find that outcrop-area change does not predict AOU change in the other gyres.
We apply its equivalent density-shift law to five gyres; it gives the wrong sign in the South Atlantic and too little in the North Atlantic.
We agree that a second process is needed in the North Atlantic: AOU rose at all classes there without outcrop-area loss.
Its CMIP6-lightening O2 projection for CalCOFI uses the North Pacific law; our result limits such scaling to the North Pacific.
Mode-water volume at BATS is one candidate for the North Atlantic AOU gain that outcrop area does not explain.
The weaker North Pacific relation with thermal-only outcrops agrees with its freshening part of the lightening.
Its phased North Pacific lightening is below our decadal resolution; cited as a limitation.
